units: a resident from an upper floor warns the caretaker that a door no longer locks
the closing mechanism gives way as soon as the handle is released
water seeps in through a damaged drainpipe above the door
the caretaker had already entered the fault in his logbook
he says he can undertake nothing without the building manager's approval
the resident stresses that the delay encourages rust in the lock
the two agree to wedge the door leaf with a piece of wood
a canvas sheet is planned to divert the flow toward the street drain
the caretaker promises a written reminder before the end of the week
the resident wants to collect written backing from the other occupants
text: A resident from one of the upper floors stopped the caretaker in the hallway to report that the door of the bicycle room would not lock any more. The catch, she said, slid back the moment anyone let go of the handle, and rain was working its way in through a split drainpipe just above the doorway. The caretaker answered that the fault already sat in his logbook, but that he could start nothing on it until the building manager had signed off. Every day of waiting feeds the rust in the lock, she pointed out. The two of them settled on a stopgap. A wooden wedge would hold the leaf of the door in place, and a stretch of canvas would send the water out toward the street drain. He promised to put a reminder in writing before the week was out, and she offered to collect the backing of the other occupants on paper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once drew their water from a dug shaft or a holding tank
a vessel had to be hauled up and the grit left to settle at the bottom
the supply was kept in a ceramic pot standing somewhere cool
these days one movement at the household fitting delivers the water
the flow no longer depends on the physical strength of whoever draws it
the old shortage forced people to reuse the water they had washed with
every loss of water was watched closely back then
today's abundance makes a seepage hard to notice
progress removed the carrying but concealed the waste
text: Before running water reached the home, a household built its whole day around a dug shaft or a holding tank. Someone hauled the vessel up, waited for the grit to settle at the bottom, then kept the supply in a ceramic pot standing somewhere cool. Set beside that routine, an ordinary kitchen now looks almost effortless: one movement at the household fitting, and the flow no longer depends on the bodily strength of whoever draws it. Comfort is not the whole of the difference, though. Shortage used to enforce a discipline of its own. Washing water went back into scrubbing the floor, and every loss was watched closely. Abundance has loosened that watchfulness, and a seepage can run for weeks on end before anyone notices it. Progress took away the carrying, and hid the waste in the very same stroke.

units: a kitchen drawer holds tools whose purpose is often forgotten
the tool with a long handle and a deep bowl lifts hot liquid
the perforated utensil holds the food back while the water runs away
its holes must be narrow so that nothing is lost
the dish rack allows drying by air with no help from anyone
the citrus press keeps the liquid apart from the flesh and traps the seeds
the bendy blade wipes the side of a bowl clean without harming it
each utensil answers one particular movement
text: You pull open a kitchen drawer and there they are, a whole crowd of tools whose purpose most of us have quietly forgotten. Take the ladle. That long handle and that deep bowl are there so you can lift boiling liquid out of a pot without scalding your knuckles. The strainer holds the pasta or the beans back while the water runs away, and its holes have to be narrow, or half your supper goes down the drain with it. The rack works on its own, over time: you stand the rinsed plates in it and the air alone does the drying. The citrus press keeps the juice well apart from the flesh and traps the pips at the bottom. And the bendy scraper wipes the side of a bowl clean without harming it. Each one answers one movement of your hand, so mixing them up only makes the job harder than it needs to be.

units: the incident happens just before the bread shop opens its doors
the cooking appliance can no longer reach the heat required
the woman in charge suspects the burner first, then the ignition sensor
the first bake comes out too pale and the display stays nearly bare
a young employee decides to inspect the flue opening
burnt bread debris was blocking the duct and starving the flame of air
clearing the duct takes about half an hour
the next bake recovers its normal color and smell
the woman in charge adds this check to her weekly habits
the story then spreads through the neighborhood by word of mouth
text: It began in the last quiet hour before the bread shop opened its doors. The woman in charge found that her oven would not climb to the heat she needed for the morning. She suspected the burner first, then the sensor that governs the ignition. The first bake came out pale, with no crust worth the name, and the display stayed nearly bare. Customers came in, went away again, came back without understanding. It was a young employee who thought to open the flue hatch: burnt scraps of bread had packed the duct tight and were starving the flame of air. Clearing it took about half an hour, dust and all. From the next bake on, the loaves had their color back and their smell with it. She wrote that check into her weekly habits, and from counter to counter the story crossed the whole neighborhood.

units: shoes must be kept away from any heat source because the material dries out
the lower part has to be brushed to remove the dried mud
hardened dirt holds water and attacks the stitching
an interior that feels cold and soft shows the fabric has taken in water
crumpled paper serves to draw that dampness out
the wax goes on in small amounts and in circular movements
a layer laid on too thick is not taken in and spoils the look of the surface
polishing with a woolen cloth warms the wax and closes the pores
neglect brings a split at the point where the foot bends
text: Because leather dries out when it sits beside a radiator, begin by carrying the pair well away from any source of heat at all. Brush the sole next, for caked mud holds the water against the stitching and slowly eats away at it. Slide a hand into the lining: if it feels cold and soft to you, it has drunk in yesterday's rain, and crumpled paper must be pressed inside to draw that dampness back out. Now the wax, a mere trace of it, worked in patient circles, since a thick layer never sinks in and merely dulls the surface. Let the pair rest a while, then bring the shine up with a woolen cloth. The rubbing warms the wax, which settles and closes the pores behind it. Neglect these small attentions, and the leather will split exactly where the foot bends, and no repair will bring it back.

units: the body in charge of water has made public a review of its network
a notable share of the water sent out never reaches the homes
the old metal pipes crack because of movements in the ground
pressure swings during the night add to the cracking
the first measure cuts the network into stretches that valves can isolate
meters read the overnight flow in order to spot a loss
a flow that does not drop at night reveals a leak
the second measure lowers the pressure because high pressure breaks pipes
a household leak counts for little beside a main split open under the road
text: The body that runs the water supply put out a review of its distribution network this week. The finding is blunt: a notable share of the water it sends out never reaches the homes it is meant to serve. The old metal mains, laid down before flexible joints became usual, crack as the ground beneath them shifts, and the pressure swings of the night widen what has already cracked. Two measures follow from that diagnosis. The first cuts the network into short stretches that valves can isolate, while meters read the overnight flow, which betrays a loss whenever it refuses to drop. The second brings the pressure down, since too hard a push breaks one pipe after another. A dripping tap in a household kitchen, the technicians add, counts for very little beside a main split wide open beneath the road.

units: the space in front of the building has uneven paving
containers there hold green and scented plants
a pale wall coating spreads a soft light toward the lower windows
the space at the back is covered with an even concrete surface
a wall without any opening blocks the view there
wooden seats and a water point invite people to stop in the first space
the second takes the bins and the delivery vehicles
one aims at pleasure and the other at function
both spaces belong to the same building
text: The space in front of the building rests on paving that never quite lies level, and along its edges stand containers where ferns and scented herbs are growing. A pale coat spread over the walls sends a soft light back toward the lower windows. Behind that same building the ground tells a different story: an even concrete surface, poured in one piece, with a wall that has no opening at all and blocks the view entirely. The first of the two invites you to stop, since wooden seats are ranged along the wall and a water point stands ready for the planting. The second takes the bins and the delivery vehicles, and nobody lingers in it for a moment. One of them aims at pleasure, the other at plain function. Both belong to the same building, and the contrast between them shows how a place divides its uses.

units: the author defends mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it
the cost of a spare part is far below that of a replacement product
the saving made benefits the household budget
giving up a purchase avoids the digging of material, the shipping and the packing
taking an appliance apart teaches how it works inside
that skill then travels among the people around you
mending is blamed for demanding a patience few people have
shared places offer the help of a volunteer and the loan of tools
the main difficulty comes from sealed making that stops appliances being opened
text: Mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it is a choice, and the choice holds up on several fronts at once. Money comes first: a spare part costs a fraction of what a replacement costs, and the saving stays inside the household budget. Then the materials. The digging of the ore, the shipping, the packing all vanish along with the purchase you decide to give up. Then the skill: whoever takes a casing apart learns how the thing works inside, and that understanding travels on among the people around you. Mending, runs the objection, demands a patience that few people have. The objection forgets the shared workshops, where a volunteer guides your hands and lends you the tools you lack. The one serious difficulty lies in the making itself, glued and sealed shut so that nobody can open it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who sells fresh produce began as a child at her mother's side
she sorted the crates before selling started
she told how ripe a fruit was from the sound it made in her palm
her first sales point was boards laid across supports
it was replaced later by a wooden counter sheltered by a canvas
she guides undecided buyers according to what they are looking for
one customer wants a fruit whose central stone comes away easily
another asks for grapes with no seeds
she now passes her trade on to her niece, who takes notes
she says she never wrote anything down and trusts the memory in her hands
text: The woman who sells fresh produce at the covered market started out as a child, at her mother's side, sorting the crates before the selling began. She could already tell how ripe a plum was, she says, from the sound it made in the palm of her hand. Her own first stall was a couple of boards laid across supports; a wooden counter with a canvas stretched above it came a good deal later. She learned to guide the buyers who cannot make up their minds: this one wants an apricot whose stone comes away on its own, that one is after grapes with no seeds in them at all. Lately she has been passing the trade on to her niece, who takes careful notes on every scrap of advice she is given. She never wrote a thing down herself, she says, laughing, and her hands remember the work better than her head does.

units: the shared eating place occupies a former market building
a single dish is offered at each service
that limit produces a quality rarely met
not spreading the buying thin gives access to vegetables grown in open fields
preparation starts very early in the day
the one broth can reduce to an unusual thickness
the bread served alongside has a crackling crust
the hard surfacing of the room amplifies noise and hampers conversation
nothing is provided for those who refuse root vegetables
text: The shared eating place set up in the old market building is well worth the walk, and that comes down to one rule the cook stands by: a single dish offered at each service. Out of that limit comes a quality you very rarely meet. Because he is not spreading his buying thin, he gets vegetables grown in the open fields, and he starts work on them very early in the day. Because he has only one broth to keep watch over, he lets it reduce to a thickness you will find nowhere else. The bread served alongside it has a crust that crackles under the tooth. The room, on the other hand, works against the meal: the bare tiling throws the voices straight back, and talking soon turns into an effort. Nor is anything at all provided for those who refuse root vegetables. None of this cancels the merit of the place.
